promise: Repeal the 'anti-smacking' law (Crimes (Substituted Section 59) Amendment Act 2007), or put it to a binding referendum
made: 2011 election (party convention vow); repeated 2017 as a stated coalition condition
detail: In 2017 NZ First said it would not support any government that opposed the policy. It then dropped the demand in its coalition negotiations with Labour. The law was not changed.

promise: Work with parties that would buy back the state assets partly privatised by National (power companies)
detail: NZ First stayed in opposition after 2014. When it entered government in 2017, no buy-back of the partly sold power companies was carried out.

promise: Binding referendum on abolishing the Māori electorates (described in 2017 as a bottom line)
detail: Peters signalled during the 2017 talks with Labour that he would drop it, and it was not in the coalition agreement. NZ First is campaigning on it again in 2026.

promise: Binding referendum on cutting Parliament to 100 MPs
detail: Not in the 2017 Labour–NZ First coalition agreement and not held.

promise: Cut net immigration to about 10,000 a year (from 72,300 in the year to June 2017)
detail: The coalition agreement contained no numerical immigration cap, and none was introduced in 2017–20. Migration fell sharply only when COVID-19 closed the border in 2020.

promise: Bring banks back into New Zealand ownership, starting by making Kiwibank the government's banker
detail: No bank was brought into New Zealand ownership in 2017–20. The 2017 agreement included only an investigation into capitalising Kiwibank. In 2026 NZ First is campaigning to buy back BNZ (see the 2026 entry).

promise: Ring-fence GST to the regions where it is collected, and write off student loans for graduates who work outside the main centres
detail: Neither policy was in the coalition agreement. The regional-development aim was pursued through the Provincial Growth Fund instead.

promise: Raise the minimum wage to $20 an hour (final step April 2021)
detail: The minimum wage rose to $16.50 in 2018, $18.90 in 2020 and $20.00 from April 2021, as scheduled.

promise: 1,800 extra police over three years
made: 2017 election / coalition agreement ('strive towards adding 1800 new police officers over three years')
detail: On 21 November 2019 the government said 1,825 new police had been deployed since October 2017. That count was of graduates and did not net out attrition. In June 2019 Police Minister Stuart Nash had called the target 'aspirational', and the Police Association said the net gain was far smaller.

promise: A $1 billion-a-year regional development fund (Provincial Growth Fund, $3 billion over the term)
detail: Shane Jones administered the $3b Provincial Growth Fund. Early grants included $6m for the Whanganui rail line, $5m for the Napier–Wairoa line and $2.3m for Gisborne port. The Auditor-General (2020) questioned how jobs were counted and called for more transparency. A 2023 Auditor-General review of the fund's 'reset' could not be sure its investments represented value for money. A July 2020 claim of 13,000 jobs included many 'previous' (temporary) jobs.

promise: Plant one billion trees by 2028
detail: 149.4 million trees had been planted by May 2020, against an informal pace of 100 million a year. MPI's tracker counts about 801 million planted from 2018 to 30 November 2025, but only about 39 million of them were directly funded by the One Billion Trees Fund; the rest is other planting that MPI counts towards the goal. The fund is closed to new applications, and the 2028 goal looks unlikely without a sharp acceleration.

promise: Re-establish the New Zealand Forest Service
detail: Re-established as Te Uru Rākau (Forestry New Zealand) during the 2017–20 term.

promise: Free doctors' visits for all under-14s
detail: Introduced during the 2017–20 term.

promise: Re-enter the Pike River Mine
detail: The Pike River Recovery Agency was set up and the mine drift was re-entered.

promise: 'Waka-jumping' law: an MP who leaves their party loses their seat
detail: The Electoral (Integrity) Amendment Act passed on 27 September 2018 and took effect on 4 October 2018. It was driven by Peters and passed with grudging Green support.

promise: A royalty on exports of bottled water
detail: Officials warned in 2017 that an export-only tax could breach free-trade agreements, including the CPTPP. By 2019 the government was still 'struggling to deliver', and bottled-water exports had risen sharply. No royalty was introduced. Labour's wider water levy also did not survive the coalition talks.

promise: Feasibility study on moving the Ports of Auckland, giving Northport serious consideration, with rail and road upgrades to Northland
made: 2017 coalition agreement (NZ First policy since at least 2017)
detail: The Upper North Island Supply Chain Strategy working group recommended moving Ports of Auckland's freight operations to Northport, at an estimated $10.3b, and Shane Jones called it 'the King Kong of infrastructure'. In December 2019 Cabinet ordered further work instead of approving it, and the decision was deferred in 2020. The port did not move. PGF money did go to regional rail lines (Whanganui and Napier–Wairoa).

promise: Put the End of Life Choice Act to a binding referendum (a condition of NZ First's support)
detail: Jenny Marcroft's amendment passed 63–57 in October 2019. The referendum was held with the 2020 election and approved the Act.

promise: A binding referendum on abortion law reform
made: 2019 (Peters' demand during the Abortion Legislation Bill)
detail: Justice Minister Andrew Little refused the demand. The Abortion Legislation Act passed in March 2020 without a referendum; 7 of NZ First's 9 MPs voted against it.

promise: No comprehensive capital gains tax
detail: On 17 April 2019 Ardern ruled out a CGT, citing the lack of agreement from NZ First and the lack of a mandate. Peters said there was 'neither a compelling rationale nor mandate'. Tax Working Group chair Sir Michael Cullen had expected an NZ First veto.

promise: Review Parliament's processes to reflect MMP
detail: A July 2020 report card on the NZ First agreement marked this 'No'.

promise: Keep the NZ Super age at 65
detail: National dropped its plan to raise the age gradually, and the age remains 65.

promise: No foreign buyer tax (and no return of foreign buyers to the housing market)
detail: National's proposed foreign buyer tax, which was meant to help fund its tax cuts, was dropped in the NZ First agreement. The tax cuts were funded through reprioritisation and other revenue instead.

promise: A $1.2 billion Regional Infrastructure Fund
detail: Established and run by Shane Jones, with $900m capital (loans and equity) and $300m operating (grants). As at 31 July 2026: $1,070.53m committed, $857.95m approved, $153.38m actually paid out, and 12 projects completed. It included more than $20m to recommission diesel storage at the former Marsden Point refinery site (April 2026).

promise: Disestablish Te Aka Whai Ora (the Māori Health Authority)
made: 2023 election / coalition agreements (shared with National and ACT)
detail: The disestablishment law passed on 28 February 2024.

promise: Repeal Labour's smokefree generation and denicotinisation law
detail: Repealed on 28 February 2024.

promise: Train 500 new police officers within two years
detail: The deadline was missed. In April 2025 Peters said it might be 'a few weeks late'. By November 2025 the target date had been moved for the fourth time, to September 2026, and Treasury said even that would require 'significant catch up'. Luxon called it a 'stretch goal'. Labour, citing Police Association figures, said officer numbers had fallen at one point.

promise: Make English an official language of New Zealand
detail: The English Language Act 2026 passed on 30 July 2026, supported by the coalition parties and Labour.

promise: Government departments to use English primary names and communicate primarily in English (except Māori-specific agencies)
detail: Ministers ordered English-first names from December 2023 (for example, Waka Kotahi became NZ Transport Agency first). English was given precedence on the passport cover in July 2025, and the school lunch programme's Māori name was dropped in October 2025. Critics described the changes as anti-Māori.

promise: Restore the right to local referendums on Māori wards
detail: The law passed on 30 July 2024. Polls were held with the October 2025 local elections in 42 councils, and most voted to remove their wards: 24 according to Wikipedia and Te Ao Māori News, 25 in some other tallies. Nationally, more votes were cast to keep the wards than to remove them.

promise: Review all legislation (except settlements) referring to the 'principles of the Treaty', replacing or repealing the references
detail: In April 2026 Cabinet began weakening or removing Treaty-principles clauses in about 19–23 laws, against Ministry of Justice advice. Shane Jones sat on the ministerial oversight group. In May and July 2026 the Waitangi Tribunal found that the education-law changes breached Treaty principles and urged a pause.

promise: A broader independent inquiry into the COVID-19 response
detail: The existing Royal Commission's scope was widened in 2024 into a second phase, covering vaccines, mandates and lockdowns. NZ First invoked 'agree to disagree' in mid-2024 over keeping the first phase and its chair. The phase-two report, released on 10 March 2026, broadly endorsed vaccine use. NZ First then called for a further inquiry into vaccine injuries.

promise: Remove 'gender ideology' from schools; withdraw the relationships and sexuality education guidelines
detail: The Ministry of Education removed the guidelines in February 2025, and consultation on a replacement curriculum began in April 2025. Sport NZ was told to scrap its transgender-inclusion guidelines in July 2025. NZ First welcomed the November 2025 suspension of new puberty-blocker prescriptions; the High Court ruled those regulations unlawful on 21 October 2026.

promise: Move Fees Free from the first year of tertiary study to the final year
detail: Implemented from 1 January 2025. In May 2026 Peters and Finance Minister Nicola Willis confirmed that final-year Fees Free would be scrapped in Budget 2026.

promise: A one-stop-shop fast-track consenting regime for infrastructure and development
detail: The Fast-track Approvals Act was passed in December 2024 with 149 listed projects, and applications opened on 7 February 2025. Shane Jones is one of the three referring ministers. In 2026 NZ First is campaigning to amend it: restoring ministers' final say and requiring infrastructure planning in residential projects.

promise: Reverse the 2018 ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration
detail: The Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025, introduced by Resources Minister Shane Jones, passed on 31 July 2025. NZ First had been part of the Labour-led government that imposed the ban in 2018.

promise: Investigate reopening the Marsden Point refinery, a dry dock and a rail link to Northport
detail: The refinery has not reopened. The Regional Infrastructure Fund committed more than $20m (April 2026) to recommission diesel storage tanks holding 90 million litres at the Marsden Point terminal. In 2026 NZ First is campaigning for a Special Economic Zone at Marsden Point.

promise: Move the Ports of Auckland and the Devonport naval base to Northport; extend the main trunk line to Marsden Point
detail: The port and naval-base move was not in the coalition agreement, which instead committed to investigating the refinery, a dry dock and the rail link.

promise: Designate all gangs as terrorist organisations
detail: Not adopted. The government instead banned gang patches and made gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing (September 2024).

promise: Make gang membership an aggravating factor at sentencing
detail: Passed on 19 September 2024 alongside the gang patch ban, with coalition support.

promise: Withdraw New Zealand from the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples
detail: Not adopted. The coalition agreement instead committed to halting work on the He Puapua report and confirming that UNDRIP has no binding legal effect in New Zealand.

promise: Single-sex toilets law (Fair Access to Bathrooms Bill)
made: 2023 election (16 August 2023); member's bill introduced 10 May 2024
detail: RNZ reported on 22 April 2025 that NZ First had withdrawn the bill. It was replaced by Jenny Marcroft's bill defining 'woman' and 'man' in law, which passed its first reading on 20 May 2026 with National and ACT support.

promise: A specific 'coward punch' offence and tougher penalties for assaulting first responders and corrections officers
detail: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith confirmed both measures in June 2025. Their final legislative status has not been verified here.

promise: Binding referendum on the future of the Māori electorates
detail: This revives the 2017 promise that NZ First dropped in coalition talks. Te Pāti Māori called it 'race baiting', and Labour called it 'cheap and cynical'.

promise: Only New Zealand citizens to vote; NZ Super only for citizens from 2029
detail: Currently permanent residents can vote after one year's residence. A Curia poll in August 2026 found 59% support for limiting voting to citizens.

promise: Repeal the Regulatory Standards Act 2025
detail: Announced a week after NZ First voted the Act through its third reading. Peters said NZ First had supported it only because it was in ACT's coalition agreement.

promise: Split the big power companies' generation and retail arms; split Foodstuffs into two national co-operatives
detail: Both are headline cost-of-living policies.

promise: Buy back BNZ and merge it with Kiwibank as a Crown-owned 'National Bank of New Zealand'; enrol newborn citizens in KiwiSaver
detail: This revives NZ First's 2017 'Kiwi ownership of banks' goal. Meanwhile the National-led government allowed Kiwibank's parent to raise up to $500m from New Zealand investors (approved July 2025).

promise: 'Kiwi Kids Grant': $5,000 a year for a child's first three years (up to three children)
detail: A natalist family policy.

promise: Abolish the Waitangi Tribunal (replacing it with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission)
detail: NZ First's version is faster and more absolute than ACT's (ACT would abolish the Tribunal once historical claims are settled).
